hook: Written by Croquembouche, this is an interactive file that asks you to accept an anomalous effect before reading, and it means it. Give it its full time and do not skip ahead, because the timing is part of the piece. If something seems to be missing, that is intentional.
whyItMatters: It is tagged antimemetic and meta, and it earns both: the threat is something that resists being known, and the reader's own experience of the page is folded into the effect, so the article enacts its subject instead of only describing it. The developer tools at the top, with switches for the timer, cookies and a false memory, are a candid touch that lets curious readers poke at the machinery.
thingsToNotice:
The six-minute rule shapes everything, including how long you have before the scrambled text stops cooperating. Blanks sit exactly where the object's identity should be, in the procedures, the experiment logs and even in Greaves's own mouth, so the true answer is never printed for the reader at all; the file only reports that people who expect an anomaly remember an anomaly, while a D-class remembers something ordinary like a clay vase.

Greaves's audio logs are the emotional center. He takes an unauthorised dose of a Class-Y mnestic, a drug meant to make memory stick, and works out three stages: what the thing really is, the memory it writes over itself, and total invisibility. For him the second stage was his son, who would be six, and his last words turn from analysis to grief and anger at the thing for showing the boy to him and taking him away again. Along the way he sees bugs covering every surface, lies on the floor, struggles to breathe, and is found unconscious on camera minutes later, while the textbook excerpt at the end reminds us mnestics are supposed to protect memory.
